lessons.title: Employer Contributions: PF, NPS, Gratuity and Insurance Inside Your CTC

children.text: Vikram is a senior analyst at a Gurugram fintech on a ₹24 lakh CTC. Every year, ₹3,45,692 of that CTC is spent on him without ever passing through his salary account. It goes to his EPF account, his NPS account, a gratuity fund and two insurance companies.

That is 14.4% of his CTC. Most employees never look at these lines. That is a mistake, because this is the part of your CTC that gets the kindest tax treatment in India, and also the part most likely to disappear if you misunderstand the rules.

body.text: Employer contributions are real money with a delay and a lock. Your job is to know when you get it, what can stop you getting it, and how it is taxed.

cells: Group health and term life premium

children.text: Contribution 1: Employer PF

Under the Employees' Provident Funds scheme, you contribute 12% of your basic plus DA, and your employer contributes another 12%. Your share is deducted from your salary. Your employer's share is paid on top of salary, and that is why it sits inside CTC.

body.title: Where exactly does the employer's 12% go?

children.text: The employer's 12% is not all deposited in your EPF balance. Part of it can go to the
Employees' Pension Scheme (EPS)

markDefs.definition: A pension scheme run by EPFO, funded by 8.33% of the employer's PF share on wages up to ₹15,000 a month. It pays a monthly pension from age 58 rather than a lump sum.

children.text: If you are an EPS member: 8.33% of wages up to ₹15,000 goes to EPS, which is a maximum of ₹1,250 a month. The rest goes to your EPF balance.
If you first joined EPF on or after 1 September 2014 with wages above ₹15,000 a month, you are generally not eligible for EPS, and the full employer share goes to EPF.
Separately, employers pay 0.5% for Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance (EDLI), capped at ₹75 a month, and 0.5% as EPF administration charges. Some companies include these in CTC, many do not.

If Vikram were an EPS member, ₹1,250 of his employer's ₹12,000 monthly contribution would go to EPS and ₹10,750 to EPF. Check your EPFO passbook: it shows the employer's EPF and EPS shares as separate columns.

Here is the choice that most employees do not know they have. By law, PF is compulsory only on basic up to ₹15,000 a month. Many employers contribute 12% of full basic. Others cap it at ₹1,800 a month (12% of ₹15,000) and move the difference into special allowance.

body.text: Why does capped PF cost Vikram more tax? The ₹1,22,400 of employer PF that he gives up does not disappear. It comes back as special allowance, which is fully taxable. Employer PF is not taxed when it is contributed, as long as your total employer contributions to PF, NPS and superannuation stay within ₹7,50,000 a year. Chapter 3 covers that cap.

body.title: PF over and above CTC
body.question: Offer X is ₹20,00,000 CTC including employer PF. Offer Y is ₹19,00,000 CTC plus employer PF "over and above CTC" at 12% of basic, where basic is 50% of the ₹19,00,000. Ignoring everything else, which offer costs its employer more?
options: Offer X, because ₹20 lakh is higher
Cannot be compared without knowing the tax regime
body.explanation: Offer Y's basic is ₹9,50,000, so employer PF on top is 12% of that, ₹1,14,000. Total cost = ₹19,00,000 + ₹1,14,000 = ₹20,14,000, which is ₹14,000 more than Offer X. Always rebuild both offers on the same definition of CTC before comparing.

children.text: Contribution 2: Employer NPS

Employer NPS is optional. Your company must offer corporate NPS, and you usually opt in, often by giving up an equal amount of special allowance. It is the single most powerful tax structuring tool left in the new regime.

Here is how it works. The employer's contribution to your NPS account is first included in your salary, then deducted under Section 124 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 80CCD(2) of the 1961 Act). For private sector employees, the deduction is capped at 14% of basic plus DA in the new regime and 10% in the old regime.

body.caption: Old regime cap for private sector employers: 10% of basic plus DA.

body.title: Vikram's income tax: ₹1,20,000 as employer NPS vs as special allowance
Show the working: ₹30,120 of tax saved

children.text: Gross salary including employer NPS: ₹21,74,308 (CTC minus employer PF, gratuity provision and insurance)
As special allowance: taxable = ₹21,74,308 minus ₹75,000 = ₹20,99,308. Slab tax = ₹2,24,827. With 4% cess, ₹2,33,820.
As employer NPS: taxable = ₹20,99,308 minus ₹1,20,000 NPS deduction = ₹19,79,308. Slab tax = ₹1,95,862. With 4% cess, ₹2,03,700.
Tax saved: ₹30,120 a year, because the ₹1,20,000 is pulled out of his top slabs.

body.title: Vikram's NPS headroom
body.prompt: Vikram is in the new regime and his basic is ₹12,00,000 a year. What is the maximum employer NPS contribution he can get deducted in a year?
body.explanation: 14% of ₹12,00,000 = ₹1,68,000. He currently uses ₹1,20,000 (10%), so he has ₹48,000 of unused headroom, if his employer allows the contribution to go up.

body.text: NPS money is locked for the long term, with only limited partial withdrawals before retirement. Do not push employer NPS to the maximum if you need that cash in the next few years for a house, education or an emergency fund.

children.text: Contribution 3: Gratuity
Gratuity

is the one employer contribution you may never see. It is paid only when you leave, and usually only if you have completed 5 years of continuous service. Fixed-term employees qualify after 1 year under the Code on Social Security, 2020. Death or disability removes the service condition.

markDefs.definition: A lump sum paid by the employer when you leave, retire or die, as a reward for long service. It is governed by the Code on Social Security, 2020, and generally requires 5 years of continuous service.

body.latex: \text{Gratuity} = \frac{15}{26} \times \text{Last drawn monthly (Basic + DA)} \times \text{Completed years of service}
body.caption: 15 days' wages for each year, treating a month as 26 working days.

body.title: Vikram leaves after 7 years
body.prompt: Vikram resigns after 7 completed years. His last drawn basic is ₹1,40,000 a month and he gets no DA. What gratuity does he receive?
body.explanation: 15/26 × ₹1,40,000 × 7 = ₹5,65,385. This is well below the ₹20,00,000 lifetime exemption for private sector employees, now under Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 10(10) of the 1961 Act), so the entire amount is tax-free.

body.title: The phantom gratuity
body.scenario: Neha, a permanent employee, joins a Bengaluru SaaS company on ₹18 lakh CTC, which includes a gratuity provision of about ₹43,000 a year. After 4 years and 2 months she gets a 40% hike offer elsewhere. Her recruiter says, "You lose nothing, your gratuity is part of your CTC anyway."
body.prompt: Is the recruiter right? How much of the gratuity counted in her CTC will Neha actually receive, and how should she think about it?
body.modelAnswer: The recruiter is wrong. As a permanent employee who has not completed 5 years of continuous service, Neha is generally not entitled to any gratuity. The roughly ₹1.8 lakh counted in her CTC over four-plus years was a provision the company set aside, not money owed to her. That does not mean she should turn down a 40% hike: the raise is worth far more than the gratuity. But she should treat gratuity in any CTC as worth zero until year 5, compare offers on cash salary plus PF, and if she is close to 5 years, check the exact date before resigning.

children.text: Contribution 4: Group insurance
Most mid and large employers buy group health insurance (mediclaim) and group term life insurance for employees. Some include the premium in CTC, others treat it as a benefit outside CTC.

body.caption: How employer-paid insurance is treated
headers: Can you claim a deduction on it?

cells: No. The employer paid it, so no Section 126 (old 80D) deduction for you
No. Pays up to ₹7,00,000 to your nominee if you die in service
Yes, in the old regime, under Section 126 (old 80D)

body.text: Group cover ends the day you leave the company. Between jobs, after a layoff or after retirement, you are uninsured unless you hold your own policy. Treat group insurance as a bonus layer, not as your family's only health or life cover.

body.title: The NPS cap
body.textWithBlank: In the new regime, a private sector employee can deduct employer NPS contributions of up to ___% of basic plus DA.
body.explanation: The cap is 14% in the new regime and 10% in the old regime for private sector employers, under Section 124 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 80CCD(2) of the 1961 Act).

body.title: Audit your own employer contributions this week
steps: Download your EPFO passbook and check that both employee and employer shares are credited every month
Check whether your employer PF is on full basic or capped at ₹15,000 wages
Ask HR whether corporate NPS is available and what percentage of basic you can opt for
Note your joining date and the date you will complete 5 years for gratuity
Find your group health cover amount and whether parents are covered
Check whether you have personal health and term cover that survives a job change

body.text: Figures use tax year 2026-27 rules under the new tax regime unless stated. EPF, EPS, NPS and gratuity rules have conditions and exceptions not covered here. This lesson is for education and is not personalised tax or retirement advice.

points: Employer contributions to PF, NPS, gratuity and insurance sit inside CTC but outside your monthly cash.
Employer PF is compulsory only on basic up to ₹15,000 a month. PF on full basic lowers in-hand and tax but builds a much bigger EPF corpus.
Employer NPS is deductible up to 14% of basic plus DA in the new regime under Section 124 (old 80CCD(2)), making it the strongest structuring tool left in the new regime.
Gratuity is generally worth nothing to a permanent employee until 5 years of continuous service, and is then tax-free up to ₹20 lakh for private sector employees.
Employer-paid group health and term insurance are not taxable perquisites, but the cover ends when you leave.
Total employer contributions to PF, NPS and superannuation above ₹7,50,000 a year become taxable.
